meta.subject: english
meta.description: Writing facts: essay structure, transitions, writing process, persuasive writing, narrative writing, descriptive writing, research skills, citations, voice/tone

facts.statement: A basic essay has three parts: introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion
A thesis statement is a clear sentence in the introduction that states the main argument or point of the essay
Each body paragraph should focus on one main idea that supports the thesis, introduced by a topic sentence
Supporting details include facts, examples, statistics, quotes, and explanations that back up the topic sentence
The conclusion summarizes main points and restates the thesis in a new way, without introducing new arguments
A strong introduction should hook the reader, provide context, and present the thesis statement
A paragraph is a group of related sentences about one main idea; it begins with a topic sentence and ends with a concluding or transition sentence
A hook is the opening sentence or sentences designed to grab the reader's attention, such as a question, quote, surprising fact, or anecdote
A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph and is usually the first sentence
Every sentence in a paragraph should relate to the topic sentence; sentences that do not support the main idea are off-topic

common_errors.wrong: the introduction should start with the thesis statement
common_errors.correct: The introduction typically begins with a hook (question, quote, or interesting fact) to engage the reader before stating the thesis.

common_errors.wrong: every essay must be exactly five paragraphs
common_errors.correct: The five-paragraph essay is a teaching tool. Real essays vary in length based on the topic and purpose.

common_errors.wrong: the conclusion should introduce new arguments
common_errors.correct: The conclusion should summarize and synthesize existing arguments, not introduce new points that were not discussed in the body.

common_errors.wrong: a topic sentence can appear anywhere in a paragraph
common_errors.correct: While a topic sentence CAN appear elsewhere, placing it first is the clearest approach for most academic writing, especially for young writers.

facts.statement: Transition words connect ideas between sentences and paragraphs, showing relationships like addition, contrast, cause-effect, or sequence
Addition transitions include: furthermore, moreover, in addition, also, similarly
Contrast transitions include: however, on the other hand, nevertheless, in contrast, although, yet
Cause-effect transitions include: therefore, consequently, as a result, because, thus, hence
Sequence transitions include: first, second, next, then, finally, meanwhile, subsequently
Conclusion transitions include: in conclusion, to summarize, overall, in summary, ultimately
Example transitions include: for example, for instance, such as, specifically, to illustrate
Emphasis transitions include: most importantly, indeed, in fact, certainly, above all
Simple transitions for young writers include: first, next, then, last, also, but, so, because

common_errors.wrong: using 'and' or 'but' to start every sentence is fine in formal writing
common_errors.correct: While starting sentences with 'and' or 'but' is grammatically acceptable, formal writing benefits from varied transitions like 'furthermore,' 'however,' or 'in addition.'

common_errors.wrong: transition words are optional and not important
common_errors.correct: Transitions improve coherence and readability. Without them, writing can feel choppy and disconnected.

common_errors.wrong: you should use the same transition word repeatedly
common_errors.correct: Varying transitions keeps writing interesting. Instead of using 'also' five times, try 'moreover,' 'in addition,' 'furthermore,' or 'similarly.'

common_errors.wrong: 'in conclusion' is the only way to start a concluding paragraph
common_errors.correct: Other options include 'ultimately,' 'to summarize,' 'in summary,' 'all things considered,' or 'given these points.'

facts.statement: The writing process includes five stages: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing
Prewriting includes brainstorming, outlining, and organizing ideas before writing a first draft
Revising focuses on improving content, organization, and clarity of ideas (the big picture)
Editing focuses on correcting grammar, spelling, punctuation, and mechanics (the details)
Revising and editing are different steps: revising improves content and structure; editing fixes errors
Peer review involves having another person read and provide feedback on your writing
An outline organizes ideas into a structure before writing, showing main points and supporting details in order
Brainstorming techniques include freewriting, listing, clustering (web diagrams), and asking who/what/when/where/why/how questions
The writing process is recursive, meaning writers can go back to earlier stages at any time — revising might lead to more prewriting
Proofreading is the final check for surface errors (spelling, punctuation, capitalization) after editing is complete

common_errors.wrong: revising and editing are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Revising addresses content, organization, and ideas. Editing addresses grammar, spelling, and punctuation. They are separate steps.

common_errors.wrong: good writers do not need to revise
common_errors.correct: All good writers revise their work. Writing is a process, and revision is essential for improving clarity and quality.

common_errors.wrong: the first draft should be perfect
common_errors.correct: First drafts are meant to get ideas down. Revision and editing transform rough drafts into polished writing.

common_errors.wrong: the writing process must follow a strict linear order
common_errors.correct: The writing process is flexible and recursive. A writer might draft, then return to prewriting, then revise, then draft again.

facts.statement: Persuasive writing aims to convince the reader to agree with the writer's opinion or take a specific action
A strong persuasive essay includes a clear claim (opinion), reasons that support the claim, and evidence for each reason
A claim is the writer's position or opinion on a topic: 'Schools should offer more recess time'
A counterargument acknowledges the opposing viewpoint; a rebuttal explains why the writer's position is still stronger
Ethos appeals to the writer's credibility, pathos appeals to the reader's emotions, and logos appeals to logic and reasoning
In early grades, opinion writing uses the format: state your opinion, give reasons, and write a conclusion
Evidence in persuasive writing can include facts, statistics, expert quotes, examples, and personal anecdotes
A call to action at the end of a persuasive essay tells the reader what specific step to take: 'Write to your representative today'
Addressing a counterargument actually strengthens a persuasive essay by showing the writer has considered other viewpoints
The difference between opinion and argument: opinion writing states personal feelings, while argument writing uses logic and evidence to prove a claim

common_errors.wrong: persuasive writing should only use emotions to convince
common_errors.correct: Effective persuasion uses a combination of emotional appeals (pathos), logical evidence (logos), and credibility (ethos).

common_errors.wrong: you should ignore opposing viewpoints in persuasive writing
common_errors.correct: Addressing and rebutting counterarguments makes your argument stronger by showing you have considered multiple perspectives.

common_errors.wrong: opinion and fact are the same in persuasive writing
common_errors.correct: An opinion is a personal belief that cannot be proven (pizza is the best food). A fact can be verified (pizza originated in Italy). Persuasion uses facts to support opinions.

common_errors.wrong: persuasive writing and informational writing are the same
common_errors.correct: Informational writing presents facts objectively. Persuasive writing takes a position and tries to convince the reader to agree.

facts.statement: Narrative writing tells a story, either real (personal narrative) or imagined (creative fiction), with a beginning, middle, and end
A personal narrative is a true story from the writer's own life, told in first person using 'I'
'Show, don't tell' means using actions, dialogue, and sensory details instead of just stating emotions: 'Her hands trembled' instead of 'She was scared'
Dialogue in narrative writing should be punctuated with quotation marks around the spoken words: 'Let's go!' she shouted
Sensory details describe what the character sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches to make the story vivid
Every narrative needs a problem or conflict that the main character faces and eventually resolves
A narrative should include a clear setting (when and where) established early in the story
Pacing in narrative writing refers to how fast or slow the story moves; action scenes move quickly, reflective moments slow down
A strong narrative ending resolves the conflict and often shows how the character changed or what they learned
In early grades (K-2), narrative writing involves drawing pictures and writing simple sentences about real or imagined events in sequence

common_errors.wrong: a narrative and a summary are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A narrative tells a story with characters, dialogue, and details that engage the reader. A summary briefly restates the main events without creative elements.

common_errors.wrong: dialogue tags must always be 'said'
common_errors.correct: While 'said' is often preferred for its simplicity, other dialogue tags like 'whispered,' 'shouted,' 'asked,' and 'replied' add variety when used appropriately.

common_errors.wrong: every sentence in a narrative needs an adjective
common_errors.correct: Overusing adjectives makes writing feel cluttered. Strong nouns and verbs are more effective: 'She sprinted' is better than 'She ran very quickly.'

common_errors.wrong: a personal narrative must cover a long period of time
common_errors.correct: The best personal narratives often focus on a single small moment (a few minutes or hours) explored in rich detail, not weeks or months.

facts.statement: Descriptive writing uses vivid details and sensory language to paint a picture in the reader's mind
The five senses — sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch — are the foundation of descriptive writing
Specific details are more effective than vague ones: 'a golden retriever' is better than 'a dog'; 'a crumbling brick wall' is better than 'a wall'
Figurative language (similes, metaphors, personification) enhances descriptive writing by creating comparisons and images
Strong verbs create more vivid descriptions than weak verbs with adverbs: 'whispered' is better than 'said quietly'
Spatial organization describes a scene in an orderly way: left to right, top to bottom, near to far, or outside to inside
A descriptive paragraph focuses on creating one dominant impression — an overall feeling or image the writer wants to convey
Precise adjectives paint clearer pictures: 'scorching' instead of 'hot,' 'miniature' instead of 'small,' 'crimson' instead of 'red'
Showing emotion through physical reactions is more powerful than naming the emotion: 'His stomach knotted' is stronger than 'He was nervous'

common_errors.wrong: more adjectives always means better description
common_errors.correct: Overloading sentences with adjectives makes writing wordy. One or two well-chosen, specific adjectives are more effective than a long string.

common_errors.wrong: descriptive writing only uses sight
common_errors.correct: Effective description uses all five senses. Describing sounds, smells, textures, and tastes makes writing much more immersive.

common_errors.wrong: descriptive writing is only used in stories
common_errors.correct: Descriptive writing appears in all genres: science reports describe observations, social studies essays describe historical settings, and poems use imagery.

facts.statement: Research involves gathering information from multiple sources to learn about a topic and answer questions
A credible source is trustworthy and reliable; credible sources include published books, educational websites (.edu), government sites (.gov), and peer-reviewed articles
A primary source is an original, firsthand account such as a diary, interview, photograph, or historical document
A secondary source analyzes or interprets primary sources, such as a textbook, encyclopedia article, or documentary
Plagiarism is using someone else's words or ideas without giving credit; it is a serious form of academic dishonesty
Paraphrasing means restating information in your own words while keeping the original meaning; it still requires a citation
A research question guides the investigation and helps focus the search for information: 'How do volcanoes form?'
When taking notes for research, record the source information (author, title, date) along with the facts to make citations easier later
Using multiple sources helps verify information and provides a more complete understanding of a topic

common_errors.wrong: any website found through a search engine is a credible source
common_errors.correct: Websites vary widely in credibility. Evaluate the author, publisher, date, and evidence before trusting a source. Wikipedia is a starting point, not a final source.

common_errors.wrong: paraphrasing means changing just a few words from the original
common_errors.correct: True paraphrasing involves completely restating the idea in your own sentence structure and word choices. Changing only a few words is too close to the original.

common_errors.wrong: you only need to cite direct quotes
common_errors.correct: You must cite both direct quotes AND paraphrased ideas. Any information that is not your own original thought or common knowledge requires a citation.

common_errors.wrong: one source is enough for a research project
common_errors.correct: Using multiple sources helps verify accuracy and provides different perspectives. Most research assignments require at least 3-5 sources.

facts.statement: A citation gives credit to the original author or source of information used in your writing
An in-text citation appears within the body of the paper, usually in parentheses, showing where specific information came from
A bibliography or works cited page lists all the sources used in a paper, appearing at the end of the document
MLA format is commonly used in English and humanities classes; it includes the author's last name and page number in in-text citations: (Smith 42)
APA format is commonly used in science and social science classes; it includes the author's last name and year: (Smith, 2024)
A direct quote uses the exact words from a source, placed inside quotation marks, and always requires a citation
Common knowledge (facts widely known, like 'water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit') does not need a citation
For younger students, citing sources can be as simple as writing 'I learned this from [book title] by [author]' or listing the book title and author
Block quotes (longer quotes of 4+ lines in MLA or 40+ words in APA) are indented and do not use quotation marks

common_errors.wrong: you only need citations for direct quotes
common_errors.correct: Both direct quotes and paraphrased ideas from sources need citations. Any information that is not common knowledge or your own idea must be cited.

common_errors.wrong: a bibliography and a works cited page are always the same
common_errors.correct: A works cited page (MLA) lists only sources actually cited in the paper. A bibliography may include all sources consulted, even those not directly cited.

common_errors.wrong: citing sources makes your writing seem weak
common_errors.correct: Citations actually strengthen writing by showing your claims are backed by research and credible authorities.

facts.statement: Voice is the unique personality and style that comes through in a writer's work, making their writing distinctive
Tone is the writer's attitude toward the topic or audience, expressed through word choice: it can be serious, humorous, angry, hopeful, or sarcastic
Audience is who the writer is writing for; writing for a teacher differs from writing for a friend or a younger child
Purpose is the reason for writing: to inform, to persuade, to entertain, or to explain
Formal writing uses complete sentences, standard grammar, and academic vocabulary; it avoids slang, contractions, and first person (in most cases)
Informal writing is more casual, like writing to a friend; it may use contractions, slang, and a conversational style
Word choice (diction) is one of the most powerful tools for establishing voice and tone: 'strolled' vs. 'marched' vs. 'crept' all show different attitudes
Writers should match their tone and level of formality to their audience and purpose: a science report requires different language than a personal letter
Active voice ('The dog chased the cat') is generally stronger and clearer than passive voice ('The cat was chased by the dog')
Writing with voice means the reader can sense a real person behind the words; it sounds genuine rather than flat or robotic

common_errors.wrong: voice and tone are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Voice is the writer's overall personality and style (consistent across all their writing). Tone is the attitude toward a specific topic (it changes based on subject).

common_errors.wrong: formal writing is always better than informal writing
common_errors.correct: The best writing matches the audience and purpose. A formal tone is right for essays and reports, but informal tone is better for personal letters and blog posts.

common_errors.wrong: passive voice is always wrong
common_errors.correct: Passive voice has its uses, such as in scientific writing ('The solution was heated') or when the actor is unknown. But active voice is preferred for clarity in most writing.

common_errors.wrong: good writing never uses 'I'
common_errors.correct: First person ('I') is appropriate in personal narratives, opinion pieces, and reflective essays. It should be avoided in formal research papers and most academic essays.
